title: Boundaries Part 2
lead: Class 14 covered how to link clauses: sentence versus fragment, and the legal ways to connect two sentences. This class covers the other two things boundaries questions test: extra information inside a sentence (supplements) and what each punctuation mark is allowed to do. By the end, boundary questions should feel like checking a set of known conditions.

parts.title: Part 1 · The core idea
parts.html: The rules from Class 14 plus today's tools form a complete system. Every boundary question can be answered with the sentence-or-fragment check and one of these tools. There is no hidden rule. The test reuses the same few situations with different words, so the skill is pattern recognition.

parts.title: Part 2 · Supplements: three questions to ask
parts.html:
A supplement is a word, phrase or clause that adds a description or a detail to a sentence. Three questions settle how to punctuate it.

1. Is it essential? Read the sentence without it.

  • If the sentence no longer makes sense, or no longer says which person or thing is meant, the supplement is essential. It takes no punctuation.
  • If the sentence still works, the supplement is nonessential. It must be separated from the rest of the sentence.
SentenceWithout the supplementVerdict
The bridge that connects the two islands opened in 1998.“The bridge opened in 1998.” Which bridge?Essential: no commas
The bridge, which took six years to build, opened in 1998.“The bridge opened in 1998.” Still complete.Nonessential: commas

2. Where is it? A nonessential supplement at the start or the end of a sentence needs one mark. In the middle it needs one on each side.

PositionExample
StartA physicist by training, Ana Flores now designs board games.
MiddleAna Flores, a physicist by training, now designs board games.
EndThe prize went to Ana Flores, a physicist by training.

3. Which marks? Commas, dashes and parentheses can all do this job, and for this purpose they are interchangeable. The one firm rule: the mark that opens the supplement must be the mark that closes it.

SentenceVerdict
The snow leopard—with its thick grey coat, is hard to spot.Wrong. A dash opens and a comma closes.
The snow leopard—with its thick grey coat—is hard to spot.Correct.
The snow leopard, with its thick grey coat, is hard to spot.Correct.

On the test, the mark on one side is usually already printed in the passage. Find it, and choose the same mark for the blank.

parts.title: Part 3 · The tools in detail
parts.html:
Dash pairs. Two dashes wrap an aside inside a sentence, the way two commas or parentheses can.

The theory—first proposed in a 1911 paper—remains influential.

Two rules:

  • The pair must be complete and must match. If the aside opens with a dash, it closes with a dash. If it opens with a comma, it closes with a comma. A dash on one side and a comma on the other is wrong.
  • The pair wraps exactly the aside. Remove everything between the marks and the sentence must still read correctly: “The theory remains influential.” The trap choice puts the closing dash too far along, so part of the main sentence ends up inside the aside.

Single dash. One dash works like a colon: it follows a complete sentence and introduces an explanation or emphasis. “The team had one goal—victory.”

Parentheses work like a dash pair for a quieter aside: “The results (published in 2019) were consistent.” The same rule applies: open and close.

Essential or non-essential? Before wrapping anything in commas or dashes, decide whether the sentence needs it.

  • Non-essential: extra information. Remove it and the sentence still says who or what is meant. It takes a pair of commas, dashes or parentheses.
  • Essential: the information identifies who or what is meant. Remove it and the sentence becomes unclear. It takes no punctuation.
SentenceVerdict
Toni Morrison, an American novelist, won the Nobel Prize in 1993.Non-essential. “Toni Morrison won the Nobel Prize in 1993” is complete and clear.
American novelist Toni Morrison won the Nobel Prize in 1993.Essential. A title or description before a name takes no commas: “American novelist won the Nobel Prize” does not work.
The study that tracked 5,000 patients was published in 2019.Essential. The “that” clause says which study, so no commas.
The study, which tracked 5,000 patients, was published in 2019.Non-essential. A “which” clause adds a detail and takes commas.

The test: delete the phrase. If the sentence still makes sense and still points to the same person or thing, the phrase is non-essential and needs punctuation on both sides. If not, it needs none.

No punctuation can be the answer. Do not put a comma between a subject and its verb, between a verb and its object, or before a prepositional phrase. When one choice has no punctuation at all, check it first: it is often correct.

Colons. A colon must follow a complete sentence. What comes after it can be a list, a definition, or a sentence that explains.

SentenceVerdict
The team had one goal: victory.Correct. “The team had one goal” is complete.
The results were clear: the hypothesis was confirmed.Correct. A sentence explains a sentence.
The reason for the delay was: the storm.Wrong. “The reason for the delay was” cannot stand alone.

Possessives, a preview. Boundary questions sometimes hide a possessive inside a choice. “The team's schedule” is one team. “The teams' schedules” is several teams. Class 19 covers this fully.

parts.title: Part 4 · What each mark may do
parts.html:
Each punctuation mark has a short list of permitted jobs. Anything else is an error.

MarkAllowed usesExample
CommaSeparate three or more list itemsThe recipe needs flour, butter, and sugar.
Set off a nonessential supplementLake Baikal, the deepest lake in the world, freezes each winter.
Follow a dependent clause that comes firstAlthough the trail was steep, the hikers reached the summit by noon.
Join two sentences together with a FANBOYS wordTea is the most popular drink there, but coffee sales are rising.
SemicolonJoin two complete sentences, with no conjunctionThe harvest was poor; prices rose within weeks.
Separate list items that contain commas themselvesWe visited Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and London, England.
ColonAfter a complete sentence, introduce a list or an explanationThe plan had one weakness: it depended on good weather.
DashSet off a nonessential supplement, in a pair or singly at the endOnly one planet in the system—the smallest—has rings.

Three places a comma must not go.

ErrorWrongRight
Between a subject and its verbThe old lighthouse, still guides ships.The old lighthouse still guides ships.
Before a prepositional phraseShe walked, to the end of the pier.She walked to the end of the pier.
Between only two list itemsThe job requires patience, and care.The job requires patience and care.

The one exception to the first row is a pair of commas around a nonessential supplement: “The old lighthouse, built in 1870, still guides ships.”

parts.title: Part 5 · The trap patterns
parts.html:
Lists after a colon. Commas separate the items. “The study had two phases: a field survey and a lab analysis.” Semicolons separate the items only when the items contain commas themselves: “We visited Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and London, England.”

The transition-word splice. The most-tested trap from Class 14, worth repeating. However, moreover, therefore, consequently, nevertheless, instead, meanwhile, likewise are adverbs, not conjunctions. Between two sentences they need a semicolon or a period before them. “, however,” between two complete sentences is a comma splice.

Which side does the transition belong to? Sometimes the choices move the punctuation around the transition: “…the first trial; however, the second…” versus “…the first trial, however; the second…”. Both are punctuated legally. Read the meaning: does “however” contrast with what came before, or does it belong to the end of the first sentence? Put the semicolon where the contrast starts.

Period versus semicolon. Between two complete sentences these do the same job. So if two choices differ only in period versus semicolon, neither can be the answer, because the SAT has one correct choice. Eliminate both and look at the other two. If the two choices differ in something else as well (a word such as its / it's, or a tense), that other difference decides.

parts.title: Part 6 · Which kind of question is it?
parts.html:
What the choices doThe question is testing
Add or remove commas and FANBOYS words, or periods, or include a semicolonLinking clauses (Class 14)
Add or remove commas with no conjunctions, or mix commas with dashesSupplements (Part 2)
Offer several different punctuation marks in the same spotWhat each mark may do (Part 4)

Naming the type first tells you which rules to check, so you have less to think about on each question.

parts.title: Part 7 · Worked example
parts.html:
The first documented use of a compass in navigation dates to around 1119 in ______ texts describe its spread along trade routes.

Check the sides. “The first documented use… dates to around 1119 in China” is complete. “Later texts describe its spread along trade routes” is complete. Sentence + sentence needs a sentence connector.

ChoiceVerdict
A) China laterRun-on. Nothing joins the two sentences.
B) China, laterComma splice.
C) China; laterCorrect. A semicolon with a complete sentence on each side.
D) China and laterA FANBOYS word joining two sentences needs a comma before it.

Name the error in each wrong choice and the answer is what remains.

parts.title: Part 8 · Transitions, names and “that”
parts.html:
Is the transition inside a sentence or between two? Words such as however, though, for example and in fact can sit in the middle of one sentence, between two commas, or they can begin a new one. When the choices show the same transition with different marks around it, cross the transition out and look at what is on each side.

Without the transitionPunctuationExample
One sentence, interruptedComma before and afterThe second trial, however, produced no result.
Two complete sentencesPeriod or semicolon before, comma afterThe first trial succeeded; however, the second produced no result.

“The first trial succeeded, however, the second produced no result” is wrong: take out “however” and two sentences are left with nothing between them.

A transition can end a sentence. “The first trial succeeded. The second produced no result, however.” A transition at the end of a sentence still describes how that sentence relates to the one before it. So when the choices are “…, though. The…” and “…. Though, the…”, decide which pair of ideas is really in contrast.

Names and titles: two commas or none. In the middle of a sentence a name takes a comma on both sides or on neither. One comma before a name and none after it is always wrong. Use the usual test: cross out the name.

SentenceWithout the nameVerdict
The Polish chemist Marie Curie won two Nobel Prizes.“The Polish chemist won two Nobel Prizes.” Which chemist?Essential: no commas
The first woman to win a Nobel Prize, Marie Curie, later won a second.“The first woman to win a Nobel Prize later won a second.” Still clear.Nonessential: two commas
Her novel Beloved won the Pulitzer Prize.“Her novel won…” She wrote several.Essential: no commas

No comma before or after “that”. A clause beginning with that is always essential. “The species that the team discovered” takes no punctuation, and if “that” is left out (“the species the team discovered”), no comma takes its place.

“Who” can go either way, and the commas change the meaning. “Students who finished early left the room” speaks of some students. “The students, who finished early, left the room” says all of them finished early.

A comma after a closing parenthesis is correct only if the sentence would need that comma with the parenthesis removed: “The tower was begun in 1173 (a date some historians dispute), but work soon stopped.” A comma is never placed before an opening parenthesis.

parts.title: Part 9 · Where a comma must not go
parts.html:
When the choices differ only in where a comma sits, the answer is often the choice with the fewest commas. A comma does not belong in any of these places.

No comma…WrongRight
between a subject and its verb, however long the subject isWhat surprised the researchers most, was the speed of the change.What surprised the researchers most was the speed of the change.
before or after a prepositionone of the oldest bridges, in the regionone of the oldest bridges in the region
between an adjective and its nouna large, national, organizationa large national organization
between two items joined by “and”the architect, and her assistant arrivedthe architect and her assistant arrived
after “and” in a listpens, paper, and, inkpens, paper, and ink
around itself, himself, themselvesthe city, itself, is smallthe city itself is small

Two adjectives. Put a comma between two adjectives only if you could reverse them or put “and” between them: “a long, difficult climb” (a difficult, long climb works). “Three wooden boats” takes no comma, because “wooden three boats” does not work.

Lists use one kind of mark. The items are separated by commas, or by semicolons when the items contain commas themselves. A list that mixes the two (“flour; butter, and sugar”) is wrong.

The exception. Any of these positions can take a comma when a nonessential phrase begins or ends there: “the architect and, according to some reports, her assistant”.
